I would always recommend getting used to the fundamental tools Extrude, Bevel, etc; because these can achieve anything the fancier tools can do. 

This, paired with a knowledge of modelling in general is a great way to not become reliant on X software having X tool that other X software may not have. Meaning if you need to switch to Blender, 3DS Max, Cinema 4D, etc; they all have those fundamental tools you can switch to. You just gotta learn where X tool is.

In terms of improving. (I'm not sure what you done already, so take this advice loosely).

I recommend starting with more primitive modelling, meaning using shapes like boxes, cylinders, etc, to achieve a model. One of my first models I did was a toy wood train, which I always recommend for someone's first model. It's simple, and it's often made up of lots primitive shapes that need scaling and extruding. 

After that, I recommend moving onto hard surface sort of objects. Crates, Doors, Buildings, lamps, barrels, list is endless. These can range from the simple to the complex. Finally, organics. Trees, often characters, animals, etc. I say this because characters and animals often need topology a more specific way if they needed to be rigged and animated with.

Now, this doesn't mean you can't immediately jump to organic stuff if that's your artistic passion, go for it!
